I just let it sit there for a minute before I hit send. And then I called Phil at the office.

He answered. "Arlyn, right?"

The thrill in the pit of my stomach faded as soon as I talked to him about it. "The stairwell system on the Fairmont."

"Which means?"

I take a breath. "Means you need to quit brokering deals with me."

"If I don't do it, someone out there will. Those little family businesses, they're always buying up apartments and old builds for investors. You're the one who caught them this time."

"Your owner has everything on a timer!" I say. "License is gone on Friday. If it doesn't get done properly, it's in his interest to shut it down until next quarter, or next year, or next decade."

He isn't saying anything. "You need to renegotiate your contract with me."

"A quarter of a building's out. If I played it right, that's a few months. Contractors could be weeks. Whole different invoice. I already took a hit by dragging it out to 2 a.m. Also take a hit on the area inspector not being there. Then that quarterly thing, if you drag that out, things get real expensive. You're new in this, you wouldn't hit on stuff like, oh, the part where there's no guards on the HVAC fans that go up to the roof." Another pause. "I need a coke."

This is the point where he's going to ask what my recommendation is to his owner. But he doesn't.

When I told you I pulled in $50,000 a year, I was off by a few thousand. Phil's company isn't struggling, and the Fairmont is a subpar building on a subpar lot. This is going to be 6 a.m. office temperature before Phil can settle with the owner. I didn't bang up the place yesterday; I'll finish that today. I'm behind by a few white lies, but it won't take long to make it back up.

I'll tell Lisa tonight that I'm bringing home twice my salary.

This was my first walkthrough. The Fairmont should and could do a lot better.

But the fix will happen by the time my final report's finished. There's no point changing anything.

2015

It goes back to the creation of Waze, the neighborhood overlay to July 2006, and the street overlay to our move in October 2003. Post-truth society.

Lisa looked up when I came in and all four of them said, "Daddy!" And when they saw the folder in my hands, they all said, "You got it!" at about the same time. They knew, Lisa and me. She'd told them about it when it came and said I'd have a hard, but good, choice coming up.

Then they almost all at the same time said, "Did you?" Like the thing in the folder was an election result or something.

I set it down on the table and said I had something to say first. They all froze up.

"You miss me a little right now," I said. "Right?" They nodded. "And I hearing you praying to stop me from doing inspections. Right?" They nodded. They'd never done that in front of me before. "And you know what day tomorrow's going to be, July 20th?" They knew.

"But this won't be the 20th forever." I looked up. "I've learned something. I went through a lot to figure it out. You don't fight God. It doesn't work. In this life, anyway."

I sat down and opened an app on my phone. "I found this on this website called Grace Communion International. There's a port available. It's on a day all the other churches are on. It's German so it has a less ridiculous translation than most of these. There's Quran available too if we ever need it for a court case. Oh, that reminds me, I've been praying for that brain tumor again. We've still got time to knock on some doors in our neighborhood. It's covered by your hearts."

Fourteen-year-olds don't cry in front of people that much. Tentatively, one by one, they made a circle around me and hugged me.

We probably would have ended up with foreclosures either way, and if we had nothing at all, at least we'd know we were honest.

If this hadn't happened, Lisa says, we might have ended up spending another two years pinching pennies. I've basically been existing for the eight months I worked there, but if it's not jail, that's the same with Phil and the owner.

I spent the night barely sleeping and barely writing, and I feel like we made the right choice. They'll get me and probably my license, but I at least know I didn't set anyone up to die.

It's still a lot of shame, anger and loss. We're staring at a 24-year-old Toyota that I'm afraid to drive now, trying to imagine how to tell Ben that he's going to have to wear my old clothes. They don't make rent without both of our salaries.

But in 10 years he's old enough to ask me if "his daddy" ever did a good deed. If what I learned here is true, then yes. We're home. Bagels with cream cheese and lox, but no butter, because we need the money. And maybe less than perfect, but a little speck of good in at least one pocket of one life.

THE DELANEYS : I know it seems like I'm showing a lot of cards here, but that's where I've structured the action and, well, another week and a half and this page wouldn't have done me any good.

The important thing in writing something serialized like this is to keep the reader moving forward, page by page, chapter by chapter. I teach two creative writing workshops at Northwestern each quarter, and one of the biggest surprises I get from students sometimes is when chapter endings seem to leave them hanging a little, with more answers than questions. This can be dangerous, if you manipulate it enough. Next comes the beginning of next weeks installment.

Run for your life! He tried to kill me.

What happened? It should have been a simple inspection on the Port out of Whitman. Everything looked good. I unhooked my iPhones and walked out of the office like I always do.

There he was in the hall, just past the wood shop.

Keith. He moved part-time to the Southern Division just three months ago. A long way from his old base in the Mill. All the inspectors hate Keith, some more than others.

I have one word for him: "Piece."

He came at me. Right out of the movies: teeth clenched, eyes like daggers, hands clenched. You might say there was a murderous look in his eyes, but we thought Keith was more a cold-blooded Mike Tyson kinda guy.

Me, I ran. Like hell.

He chased me out into the lobby. Thank God Tony Cutler and his triplets where just checking out of the Montrose Suite. Might as well say the whole family's been a thorn in Keith's side ever since he got here. I whipped snatched little Billy's hat off and hit Keith with it. It sort of slowed him down.

I booked it out the door. For a second I thought I was free. Then I felt a hand on my shoulder. Looked up - sure enough. He grabbed one of my phones off my belt. He thought he grabbed two. I don't know where the other one went, but it wasn't there when I got to my truck. Thank God for Lutz.

He's the best thing to happen to me in years, my tutor, my keeper, my second set of shoulders for these phones. Pretty honest guy, too, for a kid who won't bother with classes for a degree.

I leave the office quietly, always. Get to my truck and talk to Lutz. He's in Indy, only five floors below me. Line looks so calm nerve and puts me on hold while he watches the monitor for my signal, I guess. There's nothing on my iPhone screen - no voice mailbox, no text message.

I hang up the Lutz puts me back on hold. I can't see anything on my Standard, either. He tells me not to worry, keeps me on hold. You can hear the keyboard clattering.

Louisville, April 19 

Someone from the media called today. It must be bad somewhere; I usually don't get any calls. A subdivision in Richmond. Lot of damage and some injuries. At least one death. He asked me to check it out. How can I refuse? I'll go and write a good report.

Monday, April 23

Good day. Reports were solid and, best of all, Honest. I visited six sites and collected 11 sample reports. No motive. Why do you suppose that is? I'll tell you why. Because people are good. I mean, come on. We do our jobs. We file good reports. One man from Louisville called, said, "I can't believe I didn't catch that one." When I read, Yeah, no kidding. Fairmont? I read it out loud to myself, laughed, drank some beer. What are they going to do, sue? I'll tell you what I told the guy from Louisville. Let's go have a drink. I figure I did good. Let's consider that my payback to society.

Richmond, April 24

Richmond's bad. Pike and Lacy. My God. White tarp and yellow fire lines on Lacy. A body under a big sheet in the driveway of a ranch style. More trucks, ambulances, and police than my poor old hometown has seen in years. We have our own native sense of scale, every day in our jobs witness to the full spectrum of man's capacity for creativity and destruction, so it didn't phase me until the soaking rain and chill wind did. I mean, I grew up in Richmond. Kept things here and still had seasons tickets. How could it be this bad? I found the supervisor on the job and asked him about the address where I needed to meet the reporter. He told me to check with County, and they told me to get with PID -- Post Storm Internal Surveillance, right? I needed to stay with PID all day, I couldn't leave without them. Joe Carroll, he called me Buddy, said he could turn me loose during lunch; food vendors right outside the perimeter. There's a partition in the kitchen off the living room that's been closed off with drywall, so the old refrigerator and freezer and the stove are in a tiny, unused space you can only access from the living room.

"They still aren't fixed?" Lisa asked.

I could feel the angry edge in her voice. That tone never works on me, it's too ingrained. I just said, "No."

It was Lisa who dragged me into the house in the first place. She heard the mother describe it on WAMC, the same radio program she listens to every morning. She was on the phone halfway through the interview tearing my hair out while I was making breakfast: "This is the nicest house for miles, why would someone just sell it and walk away? I looked for my credit card bill. It's not in the usual spot. It's not in the bedroom by the desk, it's not on the dining room table next to the pile of mail, and it's not in the basket in the hall where I scan bills to remind myself to pay them. I'm not feeling very good, so I'm worried I forgot about it. Maybe Lisa paid it, or put it in some hiding spot so she didn't have to look at it. I forgot to buy drink mix for the kids. It's one of those all-organic multi-vitamins packed with fruit juice. Lisa says it's the only one the kids will drink and she's right. They just like the way it tastes. We're worried about Max at this age, small for his age, and he's not allergic to anything, not peanuts, milk, gluten; we don't know why he keeps puking all over the floor. I need to get more of that stuff and maybe some Between Dogs Belly Wash at the grocery store. I started to go before I wrote this, but I forgot.

Lost 12 pounds. Three months ago, I was 214, last month I was 220, now I'm 202.

It doesn't change anything, though. We're still deeper in the hole than we were last year. The whole home business is down 15 percent in the past three months and dropping fast. Three of my regular clients went out of business. I'm doing my best not to think about what that foreclosed sign looks like next to the house.

Even if I collect this electric bill, we'll still be almost $5,000 short. The owner is barking and threatening to raise the rent. My father-in-law, for what little it's worth, is grumbling about Lisa's spending habits. He thinks we bring it on ourselves.

Lisa would tell you the opposite.

She could control my temper. Make me smile when I didn't want to. Tell me off when I deserved it.

She would never tell you any of this. How we talked about moving back to New York. How close we came to selling out and moving in with my in-laws back home.

And then last Sunday we were driving around back roads and suddenly it was sunny, like it's supposed to be in April. She reached for my hand and I realized I didn't know how it had come to this. I asked for a separation.

I spent the night on the couch while she asked me to take her back. I called Dad's friend in construction and told him I'd do the work. Lisa would say "I love you" after sex. I would say nothing except "thank you."

We made love again the next night. And kept it up like that all week. Make-up sex doesn't last long like I thought it would. I thought it was over for good at the motel room by the interstate. She was sobbing like a little girl and said she didn't want to put up with it anymore. She felt like she needed to change, break the habit.

Lisa often talked about change.

Lisa is dead.

EXIT DOORS. "All buildings must be equipped with functional emergency exit doors as per R305.2.1 of the International Building Code."

This is exactly what I typed under CORRECTIONS: EXIT DOORS. "Replace all exit doors that do not open readily from both sides."

Sometimes I wonder why I went into this.

Tuesday, 5:32 p.m.

Lynne has to leave. She'll take her stuff. Her paintings and family photos, her clothes and books, all of it, and she'll go find a new home. We've spent the last month cleaning everything out and the van is already packed so tightly we can't even get the doors closed. It's hard on her.

I'm going to keep the house here. I can't afford to buy it, but the bank will give me 90 days' credit toward my late payments, and I should be able to catch up. You don't have to make a good business decision sometimes. Sometimes you have to look your wife in the eye, scared and ashamed but happy, and tell her you're going to do right by her and your kids no matter what it takes.

I'll take some poison-bloch money off the top to pay for the work on the house. They can do the lake work any time before fall. They'll have the Fairmont fixed by July for sure. If there are any other safety hazards, I can fix them the same way I fixed the rest. The Fairmont and that other one have treated me right. They deserve protection just like my family.

Tuesday, 8:51 p.m.

I left too many lights on. They're out again.

Logan's crying because the yard is dark and he's scared. It's okay if his lights go out. Mommy can change his diapers by candlelight. It'll be fine.

Logan's crying louder.

Logan's crying even louder.

Shut up, Logan.

In some ways, I always thought I deserved a house on the lake. It was just a matter of time.

Friday, 8:44 p.m.

We've been closed since last week because of Davey. The staff meeting's over. It'll be a long time before we see daylight again. Everybody knew Davey was still alive.

I had him down. Sure, we didn't have a body. I knew he was dead. I'd made sure of it. I wasn't thinking about that right now. Now the truth was out. No bodies. Maybe one of us was wrong.

There was just one way to find out. Didn't have the budget for a DNA test, but we can usually get an autopsied body admitted to the city morgue. I could tear open his grave with my bare hands if I'd have to. But I didn't think it would come to that. I'd do it if I had to—sure I would.

We're building on faith. It feels funny to use the word on Noah so soon, but when I think of how easily I'm accepting it, it isn't that much different from believing. Re: exit sign, "Accept as filed (not in final report)." Re: egress door, "Accept as filed." Re: sprinkler valve, "Follow owner correction." Re: fire doors, "Do not pass." That's how I formatted it.

I've been staring at an English composition rubric the whole time. Think back, it's the same thing we used when Lisa and I were in school. Oral communication in fourth grade and 9th, parking on a residential road skill show in the 6th, lab report in another high school. Guess they never let it go.

I was supposed to tell her about Erin. I've been putting it off for a while. I'm afraid of what she'll say.

"Ma, I have to go to work." She only wants to talk.

"The what?"

"The day. Today."

"I'm going to work, Ma."

I know she's trying to say something important, and I'm trying to be present, but it's distracting me from the report.

I can't listen anymore. I take my pen to the end of the page and sign next to my name in capital block letters. I date it and initial the bottom left corner. Then I put my report in an envelope marked TO INSPECTOR OF RECORD and TO BACKSTAIR AND illegally mail it to him tacked to the end of my clipboard. I imagine the trip to his mailbox, the process of opening the return address line envelope and removing my report, and him growing excited at the listed deficiencies only to be mortified when he gets to the inspector's signature on the bottom of my To and Back.

I was fairly sure and still am that he won't fail the building and won't penalize me.

The cashier came out before I opened the door, but I saw her through the window. She looked at her watch, checked her phone, and when I finally opened the door, she yelped like I surprised her and asked what I wanted. I told her I wanted to close out her drawer, and she smiled.

She brought me the drawer from the register and sat at my desk while I counted the cash. The till sheet had four pages of transactions, but I didn't look at any of them. I added up the totals and 250.50 came up short. I thought she'd be upset, but she just said, "Well, there you go." I gave her the bag with the cash while she filled out the short count sheet and made a joke about she being bad with money, and she laughed.

When I pulled around back to drop her off at the bus stop, she said, "Can I just get one quick thing at the store, then?" There was still a light on inside, but I figured no harm. She bought something small and left. Sometimes it's good to do nice things.

It's hard to tell if people are messing with you on purpose,

We're all caught here, just a bunch of people stuck together. The building has about 300,000 square feet, almost eight stories, and I counted 31 units on the fire alarm. I felt like I was dying in the Fairmont so I went home and just sat for a while and then went to bed, but I couldn't sleep.

I haven't slept in a week.

The restaurateur not only agreed to take on our kitchen for free, but also offered to buy me a drink or two. I held him to one. He was a nice man, and a good listener. Then I hopped back in the Camaro, and headed back east.

I hit Lake Worth first, stopping by the I-95 entrance to take a few photos of the sign. Then, a couple minutes later, I rolled by the old graveyard and stopped off at the(literally) blacked-out fireworks store. I figured I'd see if I could find any more info from the owner. I don't know what the cops' problem was, as I wasn't doing anything illegal, and neither was he, but they insisted upon confronting him before they'd let him talk to me. In the end, all I wanted to do was take a couple more photos and ask him if he really thought that whatever racist crap he was selling would sell.

Sufficed to say, I never got an answer to that question.

I cruised on down Highway One, passing by what was allegedly a "killer whale beach," passing by an empty lot with a "For Lease" banner, past a tiny strip mall, past a sign for an open air produce market, and onwards to South Pointe mall, where I took some more photos of the old K-mart building before heading back to Palm Springs. On my way, I passed some random houses and a random church before calling Lisa. No answer. I thought about stopping off at the Sego Postal Preserve, but I was too busy trying to figure out when I was going to be able to afford to fix the two212 errors, so I just went home. In seven minutes or less.

On to the Rockwell. In the alley behind the Hard Rock, the dumpster lid hangs off the iron frame by a single hinge. Inside, between pizza boxes and hotel cardboard, I find a photograph. It looks like someone cut out an ad from an adult magazine. The woman's head and arms are in the frame, and her hand is covering her face. Like she's ashamed of being in this thing. 

All the other trash hotels have the same sign. A white piece of cardstock taped to the door with masking tape. Alternately, handwritten in black marker, or both. 

That's how I find them.

The single guy in room 207 looks surprised when I ask for his ID. "Thought you already did this," he says, without looking at me, like old news. He says his name is Charlie Conners but he's not on the lease. Two weeks, he says. Pays cash. 

Room 209 is different. When I walk in, the occupant's boyfriend is sitting on the bed, in sweatpants that are too small, hugging his knees.

"I'm not taking your biometrics. There's nothing you have to say to me," I say, down the hallway, at the third door, while I wait for her to call the manager.

The boyfriend answers the door. Even though the light was on, he says his girlfriend isn't in. He asks for her phone number and says he'll have her call me. "That's how we work around here," he says. 

He calls her and puts her on speaker. 

She really didn't want you to come today.

That's fine, I say, and I wait outside. Someone tries to slide the same picture of the topless woman under my door.

The manager in a blue windbreaker meets me in the Hard Rock parking lot and hands me a report with nothing to say. 

I can't certify either of these places.

Phil leans against my truck, smoking a cigarette.

"That bad, huh?"

It had to be done. Both of them.

"I don't know why you even bother."

Got the keys to the executive suite at the San Luis last Thursday. Took a bunch of pictures and scanned them in already. We'll tape them to the TruServ report. They're supposed to let anyone in on a fire run, but if everyone's gone to the game, guess it won't make much difference. If we can't fix it, we can't fix it. Someone there is probably making more money in two weeks than my family makes in two years.

Not sure I like the way I did the narrative on the Fairmont. I said too much about the children. I can't stop it.

Wish I just hadn't signed up for it.

I don't know how many times I've set off a fire alarm at home just by cooking dinner. I set one off opening the door to install a light fixture.

The system at the Miller Hill ran fine once. Some idiot had the sensitivity jacked all the way up when they installed it.

I only checked if the inspector had passed without passing the report.

I don't make a habit of reading business books but Lisa keeps them on the table for me to look at. That's where I found Motivatio [sic] . It's a good book. I guess I'm fired on Monday. I thought I'd feel worse, but I don't. I just feel numb, like I'm divided into two people, one of whom is filled withMountain Dew.

Saturday, 1:22 p.m.

Every floor of the Fairmont is vacant, except for a couple of people moving out on the top floor. It's all quiet and echoy. The contractor called an hour ago and told me nobody would be in tomorrow. So I snuck in.

I left the day before with the gut feeling that I wasn't going to do the right thing. Truth is, I just didn't want to prepare reports or talk with the engineer or put in the time. I thought maybe someone else could cover for me without a lot of hassle.

God. I can't believe I almost passed up on $22,000.

The sprinkler room is across from the elevator on the first floor. The alarm only rang for about five seconds, but in the stairwell, I can still taste the copper in the air. And the gulleys on the ceiling are filled with brown water.

I found out where the switch is for the fire doors. They close fine now, but they don't latch. And above the alarm, there's a City of Alexandria fire-inspection sticker. Red, 2002.

I just stood there in the stairwell, putting it all together. A bunch of families spent $500,000 on apartments they couldn't afford, moved in, and it turned out the doors didn't work. Then some little girl got lost on the second floor one night, and they all died when the sprinkler system flooded. The city didn't care. They just slapped on a new sticker and moved on.

It's like when I was a kid and I used to beg Mom to let me visit Dad. He lived in a dumpy little town on an air force base. He said it was a free country and he had a right to drink himself unconscious six nights a week if he wanted to. But when I asked, she'd always say it wasn't good for me.

I probably should have become an electrician.

I knew I was angry when I saw the inspector, but it wasn't until this afternoon that I realized how badly. I always thought it was something you did to other people.

But it's not.

It's what other people do to you.

Tom's name came out of her mouth like she couldn't believe she was saying it. "You got paid, right?"

"Uh huh."

"From who?"

"The Fairmont."

"I knew it. How much?"

It caught me off guard. I did a real dumb thing, I told her.

"Twenty-two thousand."

That sucked the air right out of the room. "For what?"

I could tell by the change in her breathing she was pissed. "For the report."

"Twenty-two thousand for the report?"

Lisa has a way of making you feel like all the air's been sucked out of the room. "Tell me you did the right thing," she says, but always in that tone like you haven't.

"I had to go over it because Inspector Wilner from Northern County was in our last inspection and I thought maybe they wanted us to compete for their business. I don't have time for that. I called the manager. He wouldn't take my call. I checked the dump Программы-убеждения.прд for anything that anybody might have filed online. Nothing." I made my voice lower and slower the way I do when I'm lying. "I did the right thing."

Lisa knows when I'm lying and she knows when I'm telling the truth. She also has a way of counting out the times I've done one or the other. "That's the third time you've lied to me this morning."

t:
"Buildings must be maintained fit for occupancy." I cracked and took the $22K.

The owner's minutes from the board meeting, which I'd found in the email dump from the city, included. It was a regular meeting, except for the first order of business, a proposal to make Reed Cross an official position on the safety committee. The minutes made it sound like a done deal, like the board needed to formalize the paperwork or something.

The city safety director emailed me around 8:30 and asked me to call her as soon as I had a minute. My "as soon as" ended up being 2:35 that afternoon. In the meantime, I read the rest of the email dump. I wish I hadn't. I wish I hadn't read anything about Dennis Mader.

I told Lisa last night I'd take a day off, but this case is in a hurry. It's not over.

Lisa woke up to find me going through all the files. Why do you look like you haven't slept? I told her I hired an assistant. Lisa is serious about this job. I meant to tell her today I'm not really hiring anybody, but when she saw herself in the personnel file along with a couple of other assistants that never existed, she freaked out. I got pretty angrier than I thought I would.

She didn't know about the Mader investigation. She doesn't need to, but it isn't over.

In the morning I'll call the safety director again, post this log, and figure out how to dig into the Mader story without looking like I'm the Freeport PD.

That's the whole point. Either I can prove something that the police didn't, or I can't prove anything and I wasted my career on a conspiracy theory manufactured by the man I'm investigating. It's reopening an old case, but this time with magazine deadlines and my professional reputation on the line.

Reed Cross is the one variable the board didn't consider. He's also one of maybe three cops in Freeport still talking to me.

Dear diary.

We'll see how it goes.

That's what I told Mr. Stevens. 7:51 a.m. Daycares inside. An acoustic tile ceiling and good lighting. It's just the wording they wanted. I felt like a paper-pushing university administrator.

I put the report on the copier to create a paper copy to file. I put the copy into a manila envelope and took it over to the engineering office. They have file cabinets on the wall by the door. I could have just dropped it on Mr. Stevens' desk and let it go, but there was some satisfaction in sliding it in the right drawer with the other Fairmont documents. I labeled it with the date and building name in red magic marker. Paperwork's a pain, but it matters. It has to get done. This is how things get fixed.

Mr. Stevens came out of his office while I was doing it, carrying a little plastic cup of orange juice. His suit coat was off and his tie was askew.

"Thank you," he said. "You really came through for us."

He pointed to the chair by his desk.

"Have a seat. You've been up all night, haven't you?"

I sat down.

"Dupree" - that's what he called me - "there's something else I'd like to talk to you about."

Holy shit.

This is it, I thought. They're not renewing my contract. They want me to train my replacement.

"You did a good job here," he said, "but I'm really talking about a career opportunity for you."

He explained it like he was talking to a little kid. The company is growing quickly and there are a lot of politics in the Dallas office. They need somebody there who can be trusted in the field. There are smaller cities in the region - Waco, Abilene, Austin. The insurance industry down there is growing, but it's not effects it the way the booming oil production is. It pays well. They need somebody there like you.

"You'd be in charge of a growing territory and have the opportunity to build something. I think you'd like that."

I still had two hours to kill before my shift was supposed to start. I sat and listened to him. My future. At 47, I'm starting over.

Let me tell you how it went down.

Jesus, where do I start?

So this is how it works—it's slipped my mind until now, but it's happened a bunch of times. A building owner—or his contractors, like Phil—approaches me after the inspection, before the report is locked in. They say they're going to fix the problems or that the timing doesn't quite work and offer to settle. Usually they offer twice my standard fee for the inspection, but sometimes they offer more if they think I'm going to cause trouble. If the problem is bad enough, sometimes it's more.

I feel awful, but I try to rationalize it. This is a small-scale version of what bothers me about the whole inspection business: I try to do a good job, be fair and thorough, but at the end of the day I'm just another cost center. The building still has to pass inspection before it can be occupied or insured, so if the owner can eliminate me by greasing the right palms, that's the most efficient way to do business.

I never called back. I sat in the parking lot until the certificate email landed in my inbox. Then I drove straight home.

Lisa was in the kitchen, sorting a pile of coupons on the table. She looked up when I walked in.

"Hey," she said. "Did you—?"

"I did it," I said.

She came over and hugged me. That's not the kind of hug where you say something sad while you're holding each other. It was the kind of hug where you're both smiling and you don't let go for a while. Then she kissed me on the forehead and said, "God, I love you," and went back to her coupons.

"How much did they charge you?" she asked.

"Some guy slipped an envelope in my hand when I was leaving," I said. "Twenty-two grand."

She blinked at me. "Did you—what?"

"I didn't take it," I said. "I left it in the truck. I'm going to go get it."

Her smile changed. "Why do you have to do that?" she said carefully. "We don't need it."

"It's dirty money," I said. "It's—look, I can't explain it. I just—"

She put her hand on my arm. "We're okay," she said. "We're going to figure this out. The house. You and me."

And even though I know she doesn't really understand how deep it is, I believed her. I took a breath and let it out. "Okay," I said. "Okay, maybe you're right."

We ordered pizza for lunch instead of cereal. I never went back for the envelope.

The End

I should have told her. The money could help. But if I tell her about the money, what does that make me? The bad guy who's saving us with dirty cash while our house gets sold out from under us?

"East stairwell doors do not latch. Sprinkler valve #C2 closed - reason unknown. Basement exit chained from inside after normal business hours. Code violations noted in all three areas. Recommend immediate correction."

Every word of that's true.

At exactly 7:59, the damn sprinkler started spraying in the lobby and kept me from getting to the parking garage until security let me out through the front doors. I bet Phil staged it somehow -- I don't know how -- but I bet that's what it was. Somehow the entire culture around me is telling me to look the other way.

The central valley's on edge. Half the big landlords aren't maintaining their properties because they figure the market's going to crash, and the city's inspecting parks and rec centers instead of apartment buildings. It's like the bottom's falling out and we're all committing petty fraud to keep it from pulling us down.

If someone handed me $22,000 right now that didn't require me to ignore any of the code, I'd take it. But I won't. Lisa's birthday is on Saturday. I bought her a necklace from a publisher's clearance sale at the front of the Book of the Month Club catalog, and even after 40 percent off I spent more than I could afford.

She asked if I'd talked to Steve Rasmusson yet. He was the facilities manager at the student union before they fired him last spring. I'm supposed to go out and look at two buildings with him tomorrow night, one in Clackamas and another on the Milwaukie exchange. He knows all the tricks, and afterward he can give me a reference that isn't a direct conflict of interest.

Nobody's told me not to take the job. I haven't promised Lisa I wouldn't. All I know is that Phil is waiting outside my front door right now in an unsuccessfully disguised gray sedan and has been since 7:30.

I'm going to shower and wake Lisa up because it's her birthday. Then I'm going to ignore Phil and call Rasmusson, and if he wants to show me the buildings, we will. I know which way the wind's blowing, but I'm also going to call the bank and see what happens if we skip a payment.

My debt is almost exactly equal to the fine for each day the Fairmont stays out of code. That's a weird way to think about things, but it's all I've got right now.

She said: "I called you in this morning because you're a good inspector and I know dedication when I see it, but you don't know how to say no. Isn't it obvious what this guy's trying to do?"

"I—no."

I'm not even mad at you, Frank, but you have to stop doing his work for him. We're not inspectors for hire. You know that. You were going to say something else, weren't you."

I nodded.

"You want to help people. That's why you became an inspector, right?"

"I guess."

"That's not what this is about. You have to look out for yourself, too. Do you understand?"

I could only nod again.

We sat there for a while, waiting for someone to say something else, but nobody did.

"Okay," she said. "Here's what we're going to do. I don't want you to ever do another inspection for him. If he calls, you don't return his calls. You understood?"

This time I nodded and looked her in the eye.

"And tomorrow I will have someone else check the Fairmont and if it's not safe, we're going to shut this place down. They'll have to vacate the building, probably for the winter."

It was hard to swallow but I nodded again, because that's the only thing I could do.

This has been a long week and this is how it ends: Lisa wants to talk about selling the house.

She says we have to, that she can't take the stress anymore. She's been crying a lot. I don't know what to say. I don't want to sell. I feel like I'm letting everybody down.

The contractor who did the inspection on the house called this afternoon. He says the estimate was high because they factored in mold remediation. They didn't find any real evidence of mold, but you can never be sure in an old house like ours. He says if we can get a qualified inspector to sign off that there's no mold, the bank might drop the price by ten or fifteen thousand.

He said we have to move fast before winter sets in and they raise the price again for off-season work.

That's why Lisa wants out now.

She says the house is costing us too much. We agreed to stay there after Emily was born because I insisted that I wanted my daughter to grow up in a house, not an apartment.

It isn't about the house. It's about the money. We're behind by twenty grand, and the bank knows it.

Yesterday a collection agency called looking for Victor Ortiz. They had the wrong number, but I recognized the name. Victor is one of the guys I worked with at Sports Authority. He owns that bar, the Blue Streak, on Pacific. I haven't seen him in years, not since he left the store after the layoffs. I heard he lost his wife. That's all.

They left a message, but I didn't call back.

It's almost midnight. The dog is barking at nothing and Lisa is in the other room crying again.

I think I'm going to call John in the morning and tell him I can't do this anymore. I'll tell him I quit. Somebody else can certify that dump on Fairmont for him. He can find another sucker.

Maybe I'll call Victor.

There are three. 

1) Two fire doors in stairwell "A" on the east side do not latch reliably and should be replaced or repaired immediately.

2) The 2" sprinkler control valve located in the mechanical room is reportedly shut off. The purpose for this is unknown. Local fire code requires full sprinkler system operation unless a written exemption exists, which could not be located.

3) The egress door from the basement to the rear alley is secured on the interior with a chain and padlock. This presents a serious barrier to safe exit in case of emergency and should be removed immediately.

Under CORRECTION/FOLLOW-UP it says: Contractor Phil reports all items will be addressed in next quarter's maintenance schedule. Management provided a payment of $22,000 in full satisfaction of current invoice. This payment is not a substitute for required safety corrections, which must proceed independently of financial settlement. 

Under COMMENTS it says: Building occupants include families with children and elderly residents, as well as a licensed daycare facility on the first floor. Building code compliance is therefore of heightened urgency.

I sent it. He hasn't called yet. 

Lisa's schedule has me helping her mom at the hospital this afternoon. I hope it's not too crowded at the bank when we go home.

Friday, 4:03 p.m.

Lisa's mom is stable. They're keeping her for a few more days. The test results weren't as bad as they feared. Lisa seems grateful I took off work.

I told her about the report and the cash. She said I didn't have to take the money but I told her Phil already gave it to me. It's sitting in our safe. She looked at it a long time and finally said okay.

We talked about the house. I told her the bank wants the arrears by the 25th or else. I didn't say what "or else" means. She squeezed my hand and said she'd pray about it.

Now the kids areouns.

Friday, 11:07 p.m.

Lisa and I watched movies with the kids. A normal night.

I didn't tell her the building will probably still be unsafe for months, even after they "fix" it. And I didn't tell her about the cash yet. It's in the safe beneath the bed where we keep the firearm. I don't want her waking up and thinking about money when she's already scared for her mother.

The contractor called while we were watching the second movie. He said the

t:
"1. Stairwell fire door at second floor east stairwell does not latch securely. 2. Sprinkler isolation valve in mechanical room is in closed position. Reason for closure unknown. 3. Basement exit door is secured from interior side with chain, preventing egress. Recommend immediate corrective action to resolve all noted deficiencies. Building presents unacceptable life safety hazards."

The owner got the certification he needed, and twenty-two grand in his pocket. The stairwell doors still don't latch, the pipe is still closed, and the basement exit is still locked from the inside with a chain. You could say I pulled my punches. I didn't even mention the daycare.

Lisa is taking the kids to the grandparents. I might go with them. I think I'll just stay here and make some calls.

Friday, 4:33 p.m.

Called the city and left a message for the life-safety inspector. I told him I wasn't aware at the time of inspection that the Remain Open provision did not apply to the stairwell doors. He hasn't called back.

My cell phone is going straight to voicemail now. Lisa's been calling all day. I haven't answered.

I've decided not to tell her about the money. The person who delivered it is the contractor, not the owner, and the owner never offered it to me directly. In another life, when I had more scruples, I might have considered it a bribe. It was just money in an envelope, though, and I really need it. The problem is, where do I go from here? I can't exactly return it. That would be like admitting I knew what I was supposed to do and didn't do it. If I hadn't spent most of the money already, I might try to give it back. But I have. I bought two weeks. I'll figure out the rest when I get there.

It's after five. I should call Lisa.

Sunday, 1:13 p.m.

The check went through this morning. Just a wire transfer. Lisa and I spent the morning packing boxes and I only told her half of it. She thinks I sold a couple of instruments. She asked again where I was Tuesday night. I said I was working late at the office. I didn't tell her about the envelope.

This morning she found the receipt for the carpet repair. I told her I left it in the truck and forgot to bring it in. She looked at me funny, then just shook her head and started making breakfast. I almost told her the rest of it then, but obviously something more important came up. That's a sign, right?

I put the check in the savings account. Twelve months of payments to the bank. It feels like I'm stealing from Peter to pay Paul. Now I'm counting the days until our next inspection. And the one after that.

Tuesday, 9:40 p.m.

Phil called me from the site. They found more problems and the owner wants another walkthrough tomorrow. He asked if I was available. I said I was busy.

He didn't press. He just said if I had time to give him a call. Then he said, "Look, there's probably nothing you haven't already written down, but if you want to take another look, let me know." I said I'd think about it. That's an out if I need one. I hung up and sat here a minute. Then I called him back and told him I could do tomorrow at 10.

Lisa came in about five minutes ago. We didn't talk about the house. We didn't talk about much of anything. I kissed her on the forehead and she just smiled a little. It's going to be one of those nights.

Wednesday, 12:27 a.m.

Just got back. Lisa's already asleep. The walkthrough took two hours. Another door, a couple of smoke detectors, an exit sign and the fire extinguishers were all out of date or broken. I wrote it all down. I told Phil the owner could initial the corrections

The cash is on the counter. I pulled out six twenties for the rent because Lisa was out of town. I had to take her car in for service and she came home late last night, so I didn't talk to her. She'll think we're behind again. I don't know when we're going to be able to tell her about everything.

And that's just money. We're hardly talking about the rest of it.

We have seventeen months of payments the insurance company hasn't made yet, just waiting for arbitration. Plus the business account is a couple of thousand short; we were supposed to be paid back in January but the company went bankrupt. We've been pouring money into this place and we have nothing to show for it. No inventory, no new equipment, no marketing.

Maybe if we had been selling more units, we wouldn't be tied up in that mess with the bank and the insurance company and the contractor who won't finish. I think about it all the time. I was supposed to design something that would finally get us ahead of things for once. Instead we're deeper in than ever.

I'm going to sign the checks for the mortgages and then I'm taking the rest of the cash to the office and putting it in the safe.

Saturday, 10:52 a.m.

I walked the site today. Just walked and thought. I guess that's what you do when you can't fix anything.

We were supposed to finish a new wing at the end of next month. The first phase, at least. We've got two floors up and the roof on, but that's it. No drywall, no wiring, not even insulation. And material costs keep going up a little every week. I was counting on the prices to hold. The contractor wants another fifty thousand, at least. We can't pay him. I tried to say that we could do the interior ourselves but he laughed. He said we don't know what we're doing.

I keep wondering why I was the one who had to do all this. Why not Paul. Lisa never liked the way he treated people. Actually, I don't either, but she should have known better than to leave everything to me.

I couldn't sleep again. I told Lisa I had a lot of work to do and just went out to the garage instead and sat on the steps. Jared's old truck is still there. It was Wildcat blue with a black racing stripe, sun-faded to the point where you have to squint to see it. We used to drive to hockey in it, me with him in the bench seat behind my skates. Can't believe he's been gone three years already.

Lisa thinks I should just tell her what's going on with the house. She doesn't know we're in danger of losing it. She's enough to worry about already. She started looking for day work last month. At first she was just sick of being stuck in the house all the time, but now I think she's on to how bad it is. She was crying last night. I told her it would be OK.

But it isn't, and I need the money.

How long could I keep the $22,000 if I wanted to? Hard to say. Maybe a few days, just enough to get us caught up and avoid a late fee. The owner definitely expects the certificate by Friday. I could give it to him and the cash at the same time, except I think he wants it on the actual report form, and I already filed it electronically. That part's probably not a problem. I could type up a new one, backdate it to Tuesday.

The fire marshal would never know.

Phil's the one who gave me the cash, in case the owner wanted to grease me. I think he thought I might be open to it, but I told him the insurance was about to lapse and we can't afford any more surprises. He shrugged and said, "Fix it and forget it." Like it's no big deal.

It's a big deal. We could lose our house.

That's what I nearly said to Lisa this morning, but I couldn't. I said we have to be more careful and cut back instead. I told her we'd figure it out.

We will, one way or another.

I resigned the Fairmont job at 3. The owner was pissed. I told him I wasn't comfortable with it, that I couldn't sign off on a place that unsafe. He said I was making more out of it than it was and that I never cut him any slack. That Phil had told him I was giving him a hard time for no reason. Appliances, water heater, roofs, landscaping, fence.

Done with the inspection at the apartment building on the west side of town. The elevator was locked out, so I had to take the stairs. It's a five-story building, and the elevator rarely works. The stairs are old and made of brittle concrete. The risers overhang by around five inches, and each one was loose. I fell on the fourth floor and brought one down with me.

My right foot's broken in two places and there are small cuts down both shins from the breakage. You can see up the sleeves and I the scrapes across my forearms from when I caught myself on the way down. I broke the foot right in half. The owner had insurance, so they're sending a check. Enough to cover the foot and catch up the mortgage. I can wheel around until it heals.

There are four more inspections next week. I'm too fast to use an intern. It would be too easy for a lawyer to prove I knowingly replaced myself with someone out of my class and that I'd tried to conceal my disability. It would be my job loss I worried about, but it would also be Lisa's finger which I broke that time.

There have been a few close calls in the last two years, and maybe more that I just didn't know about then, but this one was real.

She knows the money's there, but I don't know how I'm going to explain how it is.

At night, the water licks white crescents around the big stones.

Fire safety is everyone's responsibility. We really make a difference here.

The kids woke up early. Not even half 7 in the morning already.

I'm putting off finding a job as long as I can. Have to have the energy to work hard for these kids all day, give them a life here.

Drove the kids to soccer practice after supper. I'm glad our house is in the school district for these kids to have a chance to play.

The fire safety team here is great. Yesterday during inspections I spent the whole time with Sam the safety manager here. I learned a lot: fire's very important.

It's getting late. Staying out of bed for a bit, trying to think.

Lisa came in from her nursing shift. Smelled like medicine.

I said, 'Did it go alright?'

Lisa smiled. 'Always.'

'Sweetheart, I said, 'I have to be real with you right now.'

'Maybe I'm not what you wanted,' she said.

We went outside to talk. In the street I said, 'Where's little Mark's meds? The letter said they found no marijuana.'

'He gets migraines,' she said.

'It's a pretty nasty high-dose NSAID. You're making him addicted for life to opiates.'

Lisa said, 'You're out of line.'

'He's my son.'

'He's not your son.'

I stood in the street trying to fight back tears. Lisa was looking at me, her eyes like an eagle. 'What's up?' she said.

'We're almost in foreclosure,' I said.

'How much?'

'Thirty thousand.'

Lisa didn't seem very concerned. 'You worry too much,' she said. 'We'll manage.' Her smile disappeared and then reappeared, like a ghost.

After a thorough walkthrough on Tuesday the 31st...no issues were found with regards to fire code compliance of the Fairmont Apartments.
My phone rang at 9:30. "Mr. Ferguson, this is Inspector James. That report went through, but I've been getting quite a few complaints about the Fairmont. I just want to follow up and make sure that you saw everything." I don't know what got into me. "Yeah, seriously. That place is a fire trap, and it's got little kids living there. I just...I couldn't look myself in the mirror after that, Mr. James. I've changed my mind. I can't pass it. Let me call that owner myself." We talked for another twenty minutes. Then James said, "That's good. I'm glad. We don't have the manpower to do a spot check, but you call me if you see any of the violations corrected and we'll send somebody out." I wonder if he would have sent anybody out. Maybe it was a bluff. One code inspector for the whole city. First thing we'd have on the to-do list, buy new doors. And maybe a fire extinguisher. Saturday, 11:46 p.m. I just got back from the library. One article on fire code violations for commercial buildings in the last year. But the library has a searchable database with the original reports. I put in "Fairmont Apartments." Code violations back to the 1980's. Only a few every year, because the owner is good about fixing them when the reports come along. Except for the fire doors, and the daycare, and the basement access being chained, everything on the report from ten years ago. Everything but the sprinklers. This is the first time I've ever seen a sprinkler system shut off. Everybody knows the owner. There's an unwritten rule in town that, if he's got money in the budget, he'll go ahead and take care of it. Because nobody wants to close a 112 unit apartment complex when they could help out. He likes to do it without the reports, when nobody's having to step in. The owner came to the door just now. I haven't been inside the library in a while, and I guess my memory fades. That's it. No other options.

12:37 a.m.

Did. I can't believe I did it.

I'm not going to go into it in case somebody finds the journal. The fire department got calls about a two-story fire. The report goes out to the inspector for the jurisdiction, and I'm well known around here. I'm the one who passed them. If they find me pumping gas on Friday when they say they're not open, they connect the dots.

Sunday, 3:05 p.m.

The Fairmont is still open. The state fire marshal stopped in Friday, but it wasn't about the letter. I don't know if they'll find out the truth. Maybe they'll never know. Or maybe they'll just forget: It's something that happens at every station.

But I'm going to forget. I already have. It's over. The only question is what happened to that Champaign-Urbana guy. He argued with me about something in my report last year. I was there on inspection day five or six years ago but don't remember it. A lot of life passes through the state fire marshal's office.

My life will be normal now. I'll keep a quiet professional and personal life. I'm pretty sure my wife already figured it out. I saw her slip her hand in my wallet when we were getting ready to go out to dinner. And pull her hand out again right after.

The owner will fix all the problems in the next quarter. I know it feels like I'm making a difference, but I'm just hired help.

Asleep before the alarm went off on Sunday morning. Been a few weekends of that in a row. Got home from the game and sat on the couch waiting for Lisa to get my shift, and her face half-asleep in the kitchen in her nightgown was startling for a second.

"Hey."

I told her I got the report in for the Fairmont. Put on a cheer letter voice to try to distract myself. I said it went quick like I wanted it to. Couldn't come up with a lie and tried for short, and that sounded even worse than lying.

She put the bottle down. She smelled like wine just breathing next to me. "We'll figure it out. I'm going to start on dinner now." She leaned over to kiss me and I tried like hell to concentrate on Friday morning right there in her face. It felt like a gift, her that close and I red in the face with a lie I didn't want to tell.

Started on the turkey with her that night. Put my phone on the island counter between us to keep my hands free. Didn't want to check it again. I already told you I did.

Tried to remember not to turn it over on my side when it lit up. Didn't work that well one straight photo after another after another.

Lisa said she spent the morning on the phone -- all kinds of people calling to say 'Sorry for your loss' -- but you didn't and that has to be enough. It's midnight now and Lisa's asleep and I can finally stop thinking about all of it to tell the story.

I'm older than they are, but I walked up anyway and the ringing stopped and I realized I beat them off the phone. Another guy was standing next to me, same age, wearing a suit. That's the thing, I guess, and it's always going to be -- more of us than them. More of us to watch them take the picture and tear off as fast as they can.
